questions.question: Q1. In the simulation you added 5 poses all captured at nearly the same tilt angle. The reprojection error stayed above 2.8 px even after adding a 6th pose at the same angle. You then added one pose with a sharp top-to-bottom tilt. What happened to the reprojection error and why?

answers.a: The error stayed the same because reprojection error only improves with more poses, not with pose angles
answers.b: The error dropped significantly because the new tilt provided an independent constraint that helped estimate fy, which the same-angle poses could not constrain
answers.c: The error increased because mixing different tilt angles makes the homographies inconsistent with each other
answers.d: The error dropped because the new pose was closer to the camera, providing better corner detection

explanations.a: Incorrect. The simulation showed that just piling on more same-angle poses barely moved the needle. Dropping your reprojection error requires diverse geometric constraints, not just an arbitrary high number of redundant images.
explanations.b: Correct. When all your poses only vary left-to-right (horizontal tilt), the homography math handles fx and cx fine, but leaves fy and cy poorly constrained because the vertical perspective hasn't really changed. Tossing in one pose with a strong top-to-bottom tilt introduces a vital new geometric relationship, finally locking down fy. That single diverse pose is why the reprojection error plunged so dramatically in the simulation.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Varied tilt angles don't make the homographies inconsistent—they make them independent, which is exactly what the math needs. Adding independent rows to the matrix actually improves the condition of the linear system. Inconsistency only happens if corner detection goes wrong.
explanations.d: Incorrect. While moving closer helps with pixel resolution for corner detection, it's just a secondary benefit here. The massive drop in error comes directly from adding a new geometric constraint, not just getting closer to the lens.

questions.question: Q2. During the simulation you set k1 = -0.5. You observed the distorted image panel and then the undistorted image panel. Which observation correctly describes what you saw at the image corners compared to the image centre?

answers.a: The image corners appeared sharper in the distorted view and blurrier after undistortion
answers.b: Straight lines near the image centre appeared curved in the distorted view but straight lines near the edges appeared correct
answers.c: In the distorted view, straight lines near the edges appeared curved outward. After applying the correction, those lines were restored to straight — but pixels at the corners were visibly shifted inward
answers.d: The distorted and undistorted images looked identical because k1 only affects depth map colours

explanations.a: Incorrect. Radial distortion correction repositions pixels geometrically but doesn't alter image resolution or sharpness. Things won't get blurrier or sharper just by running the undistortion process.
explanations.b: Incorrect. With barrel distortion (like k1 = -0.5), the centre of the image (where r² is close to 0) sees almost no bending. The heavy bowing happens out at the edges where r² is largest.
explanations.c: Correct. Setting k1 = -0.5 triggers the correction formula to pull pixels back inward. Since r² is almost zero at the image centre, virtually no correction happens there. But out at the corners where r² is large, pixels shift noticeably. In the simulation, you saw outward-bowing lines near the edges in the distorted view. Once undistorted, the lines straightened out, shifting the corners inward and sometimes leaving black, empty areas where data was repositioned. Radial distortion types
explanations.d: Incorrect. The k1 parameter geometrically shifts pixel positions and has nothing to do with depth map colouring. A value of -0.5 is strong enough to noticeably warp grid lines in the image.

questions.question: Q3. In the simulation you started with 3 poses (reprojection error = 3.2 px) and added poses one at a time up to 20. The error dropped steeply from pose 3 to pose 12, then nearly flat from pose 12 to pose 20. What does this pattern tell you about how many poses are practically sufficient?

answers.a: You should always use exactly 20 poses because the error was still decreasing at that point
answers.b: Improvement saturates around 12 to 15 poses — adding more beyond that provides diminishing returns and is not worth the extra capture time
answers.c: The flat region from pose 12 to 20 means calibration failed — error should keep dropping indefinitely
answers.d: The pattern means the checkerboard square size was wrong and needs to be remeasured

explanations.a: Incorrect. Between pose 12 and 20, the error curve goes almost completely flat, showing no meaningful accuracy gain. Pushing for more poses beyond the saturation point wastes time for almost no return. Zhang's paper suggests 15 to 25 well-distributed poses is plenty.
explanations.b: Correct. That initial steep drop shows genuine, new geometric information helping to constrain the underdetermined system. Once the math has enough varied data to lock in the 5 parameters of K and the distortion coefficients, any new poses just add redundant info. The flattened curve from pose 12 onward proves the model has converged.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A flat reprojection error curve is a sign of success, indicating convergence. If calibration had failed, the final error would remain high or behave erratically. A smooth drop followed by a plateau is exactly what you want to see.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Entering the wrong square size introduces a scaling error in your focal length, but it wouldn't create this classic steep-then-flat error curve. The curve pattern purely illustrates the system gaining sufficient geometric constraints.

questions.question: Q4. During the simulation you captured 15 well-distributed poses and achieved a reprojection error of 0.42 px. You then used this calibration in Experiment 1 to compute depth at Z = 3 m with B = 10 cm. What RMSE would you expect for depth measurement with sigma = 2 px, compared to using an uncalibrated camera with 8% focal length error?

answers.a: Both would give the same RMSE because focal length does not affect depth uncertainty
answers.b: The calibrated camera gives RMSE governed by ΔZ = Z²σ/(fB) while the uncalibrated one adds an additional 8% systematic offset on top of that random error
answers.c: The uncalibrated camera gives lower RMSE because a larger focal length assumption reduces the disparity and therefore reduces depth error
answers.d: RMSE cannot be computed without knowing the exact number of pixels in the depth map

explanations.a: Incorrect. Since focal length (f) is right there in the denominator of the depth uncertainty formula, using the wrong focal length systematically warps the computed depth value.
explanations.b: Correct. With the calibrated camera, your random noise comes out to ΔZ = (3²×2)/(700×0.10) ≈ 25.7 cm. With the uncalibrated camera (f is 8% too high), every reading gets inflated by 8%, meaning at 3m you add a 24 cm systematic error on top of the random error. This systematic offset is always pushing in the same direction and never cancels out, proving why precision calibration is critical.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Overestimating the focal length doesn't magically reduce your error; it bakes in a systematic bias. Your calculated depth will simply be artificially larger than the true depth.
explanations.d: Incorrect. You don't need pixel counts to compute RMSE here. You can calculate it directly from the physical parameters using ΔZ = Z²σ/(fB). The pixel count only affects the number of averaged measurements.

questions.question: Q5. In the simulation you captured a pose with the checkerboard partially outside the image frame — about one-third of the board was cropped. The simulation showed a warning and skipped that pose. Why is a partially visible board invalid for calibration?

answers.a: The simulation skips partial boards only for display reasons — the partial data is still used in the calibration calculation
answers.b: A partial board cannot be used because the homography estimation requires all corner points to be visible — missing corners make the point correspondence set incomplete and the homography cannot be reliably computed
answers.c: A partial board gives lower reprojection error than a full board, so it is excluded to keep the error high
answers.d: The simulation excludes partial boards because the checkerboard pattern cannot be recognised unless all squares are visible

explanations.a: Incorrect. The system isn't just ignoring it for looks. Without all the matched corner correspondences between the image and the known world positions, the math for the homography breaks down.
explanations.b: Correct. To build the homography H for a pose, the algorithm needs to match the detected image corners to their known real-world grid positions. When parts of the board fall off the frame, the correspondence set is left incomplete. OpenCV requires the entire inner grid of corners to be detectable; if not, you either get an invalid homography or it's rejected completely. The simulation correctly throws a warning and skips the bad pose.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Exposing a partial board doesn't give you better error scores; it ruins the corner detection entirely. It's skipped to maintain mathematical correctness, not to manipulate the metric.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Visual recognition of the board isn't the problem—the software can see it's a checkerboard. The issue is that the calibration math explicitly demands a complete set of inner corners to build a uniquely solvable correspondence.

questions.question: Q6. You ran two calibration experiments in the simulation. Calibration A used 25 poses all at similar horizontal tilts (±10° horizontal, < 5° vertical). Calibration B used 10 poses with full diversity (±40° horizontal, ±35° vertical, ±20° roll, near and far distances). Both had clean corner detection. Which calibration produced the lower reprojection error and which K matrix was more accurate, and why?

answers.a: Calibration A was better because more poses always produce a more accurate calibration
answers.b: Both calibrations were equally accurate because the number and diversity of poses do not matter as long as corners are cleanly detected
answers.c: Calibration B was better despite fewer poses because diverse orientations provide independent constraints for all 5 parameters of K, while Calibration A's similar poses left fy and cy poorly constrained
answers.d: Calibration A was better because tilting the board too much in Calibration B introduces perspective distortion that corrupts corner detection

explanations.a: Incorrect. Quantity without diversity is practically useless here. Adding the 25th pose at the same angle just repeats the same homography constraint as the 5th pose, offering no new mathematical help to the system.
explanations.b: Incorrect. While clean corner detection is a must, pose diversity is equally critical. If the linear equations don't get varied geometric input, the system remains poorly conditioned and your calibration accuracy tanks.
explanations.c: Correct. The intrinsic matrix K needs solid constraints for its 5 unknowns (fx, fy, cx, cy, and assumed zero skew). Changing the horizontal tilt only helps lock down fx and cx, leaving fy and cy guessing. In Calibration A, those 25 repetitive poses left fy unstable, often yielding different numbers than fx even on a square sensor. Meanwhile, Calibration B's 10 highly varied poses fed the system independent constraints across all rotational axes, solving all 5 parameters nicely. Zhang 2000 section on pose requirements
explanations.d: Incorrect. Standard checkerboard algorithms (like Harris or Shi-Tomasi) easily handle heavy perspective distortion. You can usually tilt the board up to 70° before the squares compress too much to detect corners accurately.

questions.question: Q7. After running calibration in the simulation with 18 diverse poses, you notice that the recovered K matrix shows fx = 694 px but fy = 712 px, even though the camera sensor has square pixels and should give fx = fy. What does this discrepancy most likely indicate?

answers.a: The camera has a manufacturing defect and must be replaced
answers.b: The calibration converged to a locally optimal but incorrect solution — likely due to insufficient vertical tilt diversity causing fy to be poorly estimated
answers.c: fx ≠ fy is normal and expected for all cameras — square pixels still produce different focal lengths in each axis
answers.d: The checkerboard square size entered in the simulation was incorrect

explanations.a: Incorrect. A tiny difference might indicate a manufacturing quirk, but an 18-pixel gap in a simulation assuming square pixels firmly points to a calibration quality issue, not a broken camera.
explanations.b: Correct. If a sensor has square pixels, fx and fy should be nearly identical. Seeing an 18-pixel split means the system struggled to estimate one of them. Specifically, fy relies heavily on vertical perspective shifts across the poses. If those 18 poses lacked strong vertical tilt diversity, the math settles on an incorrect fy while getting fx right. Usually, tossing in a few top-to-bottom tilted poses snaps fy back in line.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Square pixels mean the pixel pitch is equal in x and y. Therefore, the same physical focal length will result in the same pixel focal length on both axes. A wide gap between fx and fy on a square-pixel setup flags an error.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Entering the wrong square size introduces a global scale error affecting both focal lengths equally. If fx and fy started equal, a scale error would scale them both by the same ratio, leaving fx/fy = 1.

questions.question: Q8. In the simulation you deliberately introduced an error: you entered square size = 28 mm in the calibration settings, but the actual simulated squares were 25 mm. The calibration completed with good reprojection error (0.38 px). How does this error in square size propagate into the depth measurements in Experiment 1?

answers.a: No effect — reprojection error was low so the calibration is valid regardless of square size
answers.b: The principal point cx and cy will be shifted, causing the depth map to appear rotated
answers.c: The recovered focal length f will be scaled by 28/25 = 1.12, meaning every depth computed from Z = fB/d will be 12% too large across the entire scene
answers.d: Only the distortion coefficients k1 and k2 will be affected — the focal length f remains correct

explanations.a: Incorrect. A low reprojection error just proves the math is internally consistent with the pictures—it doesn't mean the scale is true to life. Since Zhang's method relies on the square size to define the world coordinate system, getting it wrong throws off your real-world metrics, regardless of how low the reprojection error is.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The principal point relates to where the optical axis hits the sensor and is determined by the projection rays, not the physical scale of the squares. Your focal length scale shifts, not the principal point.
explanations.c: Correct. The algorithm spits out focal length f in units of pixels-per-square-size. By telling the software the squares are 28 mm instead of the true 25 mm, you trick the algorithm into thinking the world is 12% larger. To make the math work, it spits out a focal length that is scaled up by 28/25 = 1.12. When you drop that inflated f into Z = fB/d, every depth reading across the whole scene balloons by 12%. Because the error is consistent across all poses, the reprojection error stays low.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Distortion coefficients are just dimensionless ratios defining the shape of the lens aberration. They ignore the absolute scale of the world. A square size error hits the metric quantities like focal length, leaving the distortion terms mostly untouched.

questions.question: Q9. You ran the simulation and observed that tangential distortion coefficient p1 = 0.07 produced a visible asymmetric shift in the corner overlay — the upper corners of the checkerboard appeared shifted more than the lower corners. What does this physically mean, and where would you see the most pronounced effect in a real camera?

answers.a: p1 = 0.07 means the image is uniformly scaled by 7% and the effect is equal everywhere
answers.b: Tangential distortion from p1 indicates the lens is not perfectly parallel to the sensor plane — pixels are displaced by different amounts depending on their position, with the strongest effect along the vertical axis far from the principal point
answers.c: p1 = 0.07 describes radial distortion along the y-axis only and has no effect on the x-axis
answers.d: The asymmetric shift is caused by the checkerboard not being flat — p1 measures board curvature, not lens properties

explanations.a: Incorrect. Tangential distortion is not a flat scaling effect. It displaces pixels continuously based on their position, starting at zero near the principal point and growing asymmetrically further out.
explanations.b: Correct. Tangential distortion happens when the lens sits slightly tilted relative to the image sensor plane. The correction formula shows that the shift depends heavily on both x and y. With a positive p1 and a tiny p2, the biggest displacements show up far from the centre along the vertical axis, creating an asymmetric shift. In the real world, if you photograph a tiled floor or brick wall, you might notice parallel rows showing a slight converging lean.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The tangential distortion math affects both the x and y axes. The cross-term 2p1·xy specifically means a pixel's horizontal shift depends partly on its vertical position, coupling the two axes together.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The math assumes a perfectly flat checkerboard. If the physical board were bent, the homographies would clash across different poses and spike your reprojection error. Coefficient p1 explicitly measures a physical misalignment in the camera assembly, not a bend in the board.

questions.question: Q10. In the simulation you ran two complete calibrations. Calibration X gave reprojection error = 0.35 px with fx = 702, fy = 699, cx = 160, cy = 121, k1 = -0.31. Calibration Y gave reprojection error = 1.9 px with fx = 698, fy = 700, cx = 159, cy = 122, k1 = -0.30. For a depth measurement task requiring ±5 mm accuracy at Z = 1.5 m with B = 12 cm and sigma = 1 px, which calibration would you use and what would the expected depth RMSE be?

answers.a: Calibration Y because its focal length values are closer to 700 px which is the standard camera focal length
answers.b: Both calibrations give the same depth RMSE because their K matrix values are nearly identical
answers.c: Calibration X because its lower reprojection error means its K matrix is more accurately estimated, and the depth RMSE from sigma = 1 px noise at these settings is ΔZ = 1.5² × 1 / (700 × 0.12) ≈ 2.7 cm — which does not meet the ±5 mm requirement regardless of which calibration is used
answers.d: Calibration Y because higher reprojection error means the calibration was computed from more diverse poses, making it more robust

explanations.a: Incorrect. Cameras don't share a universal 'standard' focal length of 700 px—it relies entirely on the individual lens and sensor. You shouldn't pick between identical-looking K matrices based on an arbitrary number; you look at the reprojection error.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Although the K matrices look similar, the underlying question requires a deeper math check. Even using the better calibration, the depth RMSE hits about 2.7 cm, completely failing the ±5 mm requirement. The physics limitation is a bigger deal than the minor difference between the calibrations.
explanations.c: Correct. You'd pick Calibration X since its 0.35 px reprojection error proves it's a more accurate model. But the critical takeaway here is the math: ΔZ = Z²σ/(fB) = (1.5² × 1)/(700 × 0.12) ≈ 2.7 cm. Even with a stellar calibration, your baseline setup inherently produces 2.7 cm of noise, blowing right past the ±5 mm accuracy requirement. No calibration tweak can fix an inadequate physical setup. Zhang 2000 calibration accuracy analysis
explanations.d: Incorrect. A higher reprojection error doesn't signal robustness; it signals poor parameter estimation, usually caused by fewer or weaker poses. Always aim for a lower reprojection error to ensure accurate parameter estimation.
